messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Moshe is a 63-year-old rabbi who came to the United States as a young man after fleeing violent civil conflict in his country of origin. He presents now with a PCL-5 score of 57, seeking help for the first time after decades of managing — or believing he was managing — on his own.

The events that shaped his current presentation occurred when Moshe was in his late twenties, during a period of forced displacement. He and a group of others were detained at a checkpoint by armed soldiers. There was shouting — sustained, chaotic, aimed directly at him and those around him — and at one point a soldier grabbed him by the collar without warning, pressing a rifle barrel against his chest. He was eventually released, but two people he had been travelling with were not. He has never spoken about this publicly, not even in the pastoral context where he has spent thirty years helping others speak about their pain.

In the years that followed, Moshe built a life of considerable structure and meaning. He leads a mid-sized congregation, teaches regularly, and is in a long-term relationship with a partner who describes him as warm but unreachable. The symptoms did not arrive all at once. They accumulated quietly, like sediment. He noticed, perhaps five or six years after arriving in the United States, that he could no longer sit with his back to a door. He began arriving early to synagogue board meetings so he could take the chair nearest the exit. Over time this extended to restaurants, waiting rooms, and family gatherings — he now feels genuinely safe only at home, in a specific chair, in a room he can see entirely. He has arranged his office at the synagogue in the same way.

The triggers that most reliably fracture his composure are the ones that echo the checkpoint: a hand placed unexpectedly on his shoulder during a congregational embrace, the sight of a security guard's holstered weapon at a community event, or raised voices in any context — even celebratory ones. When these occur, his body floods with a response that he finds deeply distressing and deeply shaming. He has come to believe that his body is working against him, that it is reacting as though the checkpoint is still happening, and this belief — that he cannot trust his own physiology — feeds a broader conviction that he cannot rely on himself at all. These appraisals of personal unreliability then sharpen his vigilance: if he cannot trust himself to remain calm or rational, the environment must be controlled instead, and so his scanning for threat intensifies, and the range of places and situations that feel tolerable continues to narrow. The narrowing, in turn, means he encounters triggers more reliably in the few contexts he cannot avoid — the synagogue most of all, where unexpected touch is a feature of pastoral life and where, on two recent occasions, raised voices during a congregational dispute sent him into a state of acute distress that he concealed with visible effort.

When a trigger does break through, Moshe's immediate response is to pull his attention elsewhere — to a text he is preparing, a logistical task, anything that provides cognitive cover. This distraction offers short-term relief but leaves the underlying activation unprocessed, so that the next trigger finds him already primed. He also engages in what he himself named in the second session as "punishment thinking" — a quiet, persistent conviction that he deserves to suffer for what happened, that a stronger or better man would have intervened, that someone else would have stopped it. This self-punishing stance has made it nearly impossible to allow emotional closeness with his partner, whom he loves but keeps at a careful distance, offering presence without vulnerability. The avoidance of intimacy, and the ongoing self-punishment, have paradoxically kept the traumatic material close and unresolved, sustaining the appraisals of personal failure that make the threat monitoring feel not only necessary but deserved.

What finally brought Moshe in was a moment three months ago when a young congregant placed both hands on his shoulders in gratitude, and Moshe — a man known for his steadiness — flinched so visibly that the congregant apologised. He drove home in silence. What he most fears is that he will never be the person his community believes him to be. What he most hopes, though he has not yet said this directly, is that he might be allowed to put something down.
